extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103, including when to apply 'obvious to try', teaching/suggestion/motivation, reasonable expectation of success, and how to treat claim limitations and prior art. Intended to direct Office personnel in articulating factual findings and legal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of 'obvious to try' rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'obvious to try' rationale can properly support obviousness only when the claimed solution would have been selected from a finite number of potential solutions known to persons of ordinary skill and when the result would have been reasonably predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should not apply 'obvious to try' when, considering all evidence, the outcome would not have been reasonably predictable and the inventor would not have had a reasonable expectation of success. Cite Rolls-Royce and Sanders/Sanofi examples: where options were not known or the change would not have presented itself as an option, 'obvious to try' is inappropriate. Conversely, when a finite number of identified, predictable solutions exist (Perfect Web), 'obvious to try' may lead to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results can rebut prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results (e.g., unpredicted therapeutic advantages) can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicants present credible evidence that the claimed invention produced unexpected properties (e.g., Sanofi D-isomer therapeutic advantage with low toxicity), examiners must consider that evidence; such evidence may prevent sustaining an obviousness rejection even where a prima facie case exists. The district court’s finding based on expert testimony may be dispositive if clear and convincing evidence of nonobviousness is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another
rubrics_metrics.description: A known device/method/product in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or different field if the variations would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reject based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and explicitly articulate findings: (1) scope/content of prior art included a similar or analogous device; (2) design incentives or market forces would prompt adaptation; (3) differences between claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations/principles; (4) a person of ordinary skill could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable; and (5) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness can be established by combining or modifying prior art teachings where there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must resolve Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) a finding of some teaching/suggestion/motivation in references or general knowledge to modify/combine; (2) a finding of reasonable expectation of success; and (3) any additional Graham findings needed. The motivation may be explicit or implicit (e.g., nature of the problem or desire to improve commercial opportunities). The TSM test is flexible and is a guard against hindsight; an explicit written motivation is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh conflicting teachings of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When teachings of two or more prior art references conflict, the examiner must weigh the suggestive power of each reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the degree to which one reference discredits another and the extent to which each would have suggested solutions to one of ordinary skill. Analyze whether conflicting references would deter or encourage the proposed combination (see In re Young example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of references must yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that references can be combined does not establish prima facie obviousness unless the results of the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow KSR: predictable variations that a skilled artisan could implement typically render patentability barred under §103. Where unpredictability exists, a prima facie case of obviousness may not be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive statements of capability are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere statement that the claimed invention was within the capabilities of one of ordinary skill is not sufficient to establish prima facie obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; examiners must provide articulated reasoning and objective reasons to combine references (see Ex parte Levengood and KSR quoting In re Kahn). Provide factual underpinnings rather than conclusory claims that 'all aspects were individually known.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot render prior art unsatisfactory for intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed modification would make the prior art device inoperative or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there is no suggestion or motivation to make that modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the modification would defeat the prior art’s purpose (In re Gordon example). If turning or modifying would make the device inoperable, that weighs against motivation to combine. Simplicity of prior art does not automatically teach away from added functionality; consider full context (In re Dance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot change the principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed modification or combination that would change the basic principle under which a prior art reference operates cannot render the claim prima facie obvious based on that reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If achieving the claimed invention would require substantial reconstruction/redesign and a change in the basic operating principle of the primary reference, the suggested combination is not a proper basis for obviousness (In re Ratti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success required for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To sustain a prima facie obviousness rejection where there is motivation to combine or modify prior art, there must also have been a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness requires at least some predictability that the modification/combination would work (Merck, Ex parte Blanc). Evidence of unpredictability (e.g., inability to scale or uncertainty in field) may support nonobviousness (In re Rinehart, Amgen v. Chugai). Consider art-specific predictability and provide record support for expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of predictability assessed at time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictability (and reasonable expectation of success) must be evaluated as of the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time would have been motivated to combine/modify references with a reasonable expectation of success (Ex parte Erlich). Later developments do not retroactively make earlier combinations predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all claim limitations in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All words in a claim must be considered in judging patentability against the prior art; dependent claims inherit patentability status from independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an independent claim is nonobvious, dependent claims are nonobvious (In re Wilson; In re Fine). Do not ignore claim limitations; analyze each limitation in the context of the prior art combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered and can mandate rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim term admits multiple interpretations and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should reject the claim as indefinite and also reject over the prior art as applicable under that interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claim language lacks a reasonably definite meaning, issue a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph) and address prior art under the interpretation that makes the claim unpatentable (Ex parte Ionescu). Compare to cases where no definite meaning can be ascribed (In re Wilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense may inform obviousness only with reasoned explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense can inform analysis of obviousness but must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation and not mere conclusory generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply common sense when supported by sufficient reasoning and factual basis (Perfect Web; In re Bozek; In re Zurko). Identification of a 'specific hint or suggestion' in a reference is not always required, but a reasoned explanation is necessary to avoid hindsight. Use precedent (DyStar, In re Kahn) to frame when implicit motivation/common sense is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of multiple alternatives does not necessarily teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosure of more than one alternative does not constitute teaching away from any of those alternatives unless the disclosure criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference discloses several alternatives, that mere disclosure does not prevent the examiner from finding motivation to combine; only explicit discouragement or criticism of an alternative could be 'teaching away' (In re Fulton). Consider whether the prior art as a whole suggests desirability of the claimed combination.
